title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Prince Andrew needed to see the district marshal of the nobility in connection with his son's Ryazan estate. This marshal was Count Ilya Rostov, and in the middle of May, Prince Andrew went to visit him.
It was now hot spring weather. The forest was fully green. It was dusty and so warm that passing any water made you long to bathe.

Prince Andrew, preoccupied and gloomy about the business he needed to discuss with the marshal, was driving up the avenue to the Rostovs' house at Otradnoe. He heard merry girlish cries from behind some trees to the right and saw a group of girls running across the path of his carriage. Ahead of the others, nearest to him, ran a dark-haired, remarkably slim, pretty girl in a yellow cotton dress with a white kerchief on her head, from under which loose locks of hair had escaped. The girl was shouting something but, seeing a stranger, ran back laughing without looking at him.

Suddenly, and he didn't know why, he felt a pang. The day was so beautiful, the sun so bright, everything around so cheerful — and that slim, pretty girl didn't know or care that he existed. She was content and happy in her own separate — probably silly — but bright and joyful life. "What is she so glad about? What is she thinking of? Not about military regulations or the arrangement of the Ryazan serfs' rents. What is she thinking? Why is she so happy?" Prince Andrew asked himself with involuntary curiosity.

In 1809 Count Ilya Rostov was living at Otradnoe just as in previous years — entertaining nearly the whole province with hunts, theatricals, dinners, and music. He was glad to see Prince Andrew, as he was to see any new visitor, and insisted he stay the night.

During the tedious day, in the course of which he was entertained by his elderly hosts and the more important visitors — the old count's house was packed in anticipation of a name-day celebration — Prince Andrew kept glancing at Natasha, who was gay and laughing among the younger guests, and each time he asked himself: "What is she thinking about? Why is she so happy?"

That night, alone in unfamiliar surroundings, he was long unable to sleep. He read for a while, then put out his candle — then relit it. It was hot in the room, with the shutters closed. He was annoyed at the foolish old man (as he called Rostov) who had kept him there by insisting that some necessary documents hadn't arrived from town, and he was annoyed at himself for having stayed.

He got up and went to the window to open it. The moment he opened the shutters, the moonlight — as if it had been waiting for this — flooded into the room. He opened the casement. The night was cool, bright, and perfectly still. Just below the window stood a row of pollard trees, black on one side, silvery on the other. Beneath them grew some kind of lush, wet, bushy vegetation with silver-touched leaves and stems here and there. Further off, beyond the dark trees, a roof glistened with dew; to the right rose a great leafy tree with brilliantly white trunk and branches, and above it shone the moon, nearly full, in a pale, almost starless spring sky. Prince Andrew leaned his elbows on the window ledge and let his gaze rest on that sky.
His room was on the first floor. Those in the rooms above were awake too. He heard female voices overhead.
"Just once more," said a girlish voice above him that Prince Andrew recognized at once.
"But when are you going to bed?" replied another voice.
"I won't! I can't sleep — what's the use? Come on, one last time."
Two girlish voices sang a musical passage — the ending of some song.
"Oh, how lovely! Now go to sleep — that's it."

"You go to sleep, but I can't," said the first voice, coming nearer to the window. She was evidently leaning right out, because the rustle of her dress and even her breathing could be heard. Everything was stone-still — like the moon and its light and the shadows. Prince Andrew, too, dared not stir, afraid of revealing his presence.

"Sonya! Sonya!" he heard the first voice again. "Oh, how can you sleep! Just look how gorgeous it is! Oh, how gorgeous! Wake up, Sonya!" she said, almost in tears. "There has never, never been such a beautiful night!"
Sonya murmured something reluctant in reply.

"Come look at the moon! Oh, how lovely! Come here, darling, sweetheart, come here! See? I feel like crouching down on my heels and hugging my knees like this, pulling tight — as tight as I can — and flying away! Like this..."
"Careful — you'll fall out."
He heard the sound of a scuffle and Sonya's disapproving voice: "It's past one o'clock."
"Oh, you just ruin everything. Fine — go, go!"
Again all was silent, but Prince Andrew knew she was still sitting there. From time to time he heard a soft rustle, and once a sigh.
"Oh God! Oh God! What does it mean?" she suddenly exclaimed. "Well, off to bed then, if I must!" And she slammed the window shut.

"I might as well not exist for her!" thought Prince Andrew as he listened, for some reason expecting — and fearing — that she might say something about him. "There she is again! As if it were on purpose," he thought.

In his soul there suddenly arose such an unexpected turmoil of youthful thoughts and hopes — so contrary to the whole direction of his life — that, unable to make sense of his own state, he lay down and fell asleep at once.
